cards.explanation: The message they've heard from the beginning is that we should love one another. The writer says, “This is the message you have heard from the beginning: We should love one another.” It isn't a fresh idea they're hearing for the first time. They've had it since the start, and they still get to practice it today.

Evil goes in the first blank, and righteous goes in the second. The writer says Cain's own deeds were evil. Cain, Adam and Eve's son (Genesis 4:1), belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. It's a heavy verse, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit. Righteous is the writer's word for the deeds of Cain's brother, and I think this part hurts to read, friends, because his deeds were righteous and Cain killed him anyway.

The answer is False. The writer says, “So do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you.” He doesn't tell them the world will love them. He tells them not to be surprised if it hates them. A heads-up like that beats getting caught off guard.

Love is the word, friends. The writer says, “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers.” It's how we know. Not a feeling we hope is true, but love showing up toward our brothers.

The writer calls everyone who hates his brother a murderer. He says, “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer…” It's a strong thing to say, and he says it plainly. He adds that eternal life does not reside in a murderer.

The writer says we know what love is because Jesus laid down His life for us. He says, “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us…” He doesn't point to a definition. He points to what Jesus did. Then he says we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.

The answer is True, friends. The writer says, “…we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.” He says it right after pointing to Jesus laying down His life for us. It's a big ask, and the writer says it straight.

The writer asks, “…how can the love of God abide in him?” He's talking about the one who has earthly possessions, sees his brother in need and withholds his compassion. He lets the question hang there on purpose, I think, and it's a good one for all of us to chew on.

The writer tells his little children to love in action and truth. He says, “Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.” Love that shows up and does something. That kind of love doesn't need a speech.
The answer is False. The writer says, “And by this we will know that we belong to the truth…” Not the world, the truth. It comes right after he tells his little children to love in action and truth.

The writer says God is greater than our hearts. He says, “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things.” Our hearts can be loud, but they don't get the last word. God is greater.
The answer is False. The writer says, “Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God…” He doesn't say we should still be afraid. He says we have confidence.

The reason the writer gives is that we keep His commandments and do what pleases Him. He says we will receive from God whatever we ask, “…because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight.” Both parts are in the verse, friends.

The answer is True, friends. The writer says, “And this is His commandment: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ…” Then he adds that we should love one another just as He commanded us. Two parts, one commandment.

The writer says we know God remains in us by the Spirit He has given us. He says, “And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.” The Spirit is a gift God gave, and that's how we know. I spent years in a junk drawer wondering if anybody remembered me, so I can tell you a gift like that means a lot.
